value: branches incubated with 1,8-cineole for 24 h received approximately half the herbivore-damage level (LS means difference 14.7, P = 0.01)
method: field assay: one branch of ~100 leaves per plant enclosed in a clear plastic bag with a 1 cm2 filter paper square carrying 1 ml of one volatile compound for 24 h, then bag and paper removed; leaves with herbivore damage counted through the season; GLM on log-transformed data with Dunnett's test against the control
conditions: Wild sagebrush along Sagehen Creek (39 26.7N, 120 12.9W), field experiment in 2011; each chemical treatment on 30 different plants, plants at least 5 m apart; controls bagged with a clean filter paper square; control branches had about 30% of leaves with some herbivore damage by the end of the season. Four compounds tested; the compounds together significantly affected damage (F 4,144 = 2.47, P = 0.047). Companion results in the same test: beta-caryophyllene branches tended to receive less herbivory but the difference was marginally not significant (LS means difference 11.1, P = 0.08); alpha-pinene (difference 7.0, P = 0.43) and borneol (difference 6.6, P = 0.48) were not statistically distinguishable from controls. Compounds were applied singly as pure chemicals, not as a blend; the abstract's wording that cineol or caryophyllene 'generally suffered less damage' rests on the cineole result alone being significant.

value: monoterpene emissions from the herbivore-treated plant rose from 48.1 +/- 9.8 to 2080 +/- 383 ug m-2 h-1 during active feeding
method: dynamic-enclosure measurement of whole-plant monoterpene emission before and during 48 h of feeding by adult large pine weevils (Hylobius abietis)
conditions: Seven-year-old Scots pine saplings grown in 7.5 L pots (sand, garden soil, peat 1:1:1), moved indoors at least 24 h before each of four experiments run in summer 2015; each experiment had one treatment plant and one control plant, each in an approximately 70 L Tedlar dynamic enclosure at the trunk; treatment = four adult large pine weevils (Hylobius abietis) in a mesh foam enclosure left on the treatment plant for 48 h, control = an empty foam enclosure; emissions by PTR-ToF-MS with Tenax cartridge samples. Control plant monoterpene emissions were 56.1 and 39.7 ug m-2 h-1 in the pre-treatment and feeding phases; control sesquiterpene emissions were 23.1 and 11.2. Monoterpene post-treatment emission was 435.5 +/- 139.1 (lower than during feeding but above pre-treatment) and sesquiterpene post-treatment 17.8 +/- 5.2. t-tests: treatment differed from control during feeding and post-treatment, with no significant difference pre-treatment; the text reports the monoterpene feeding contrast as t = 5.329 and the sesquiterpene feeding contrast as t = -2.5753 (sign as printed). In experiment 2 high emissions persisted after the weevils were removed. The paper's aim is secondary organic aerosol yield, with the herbivore used to stress the trees.
